videos.title: Why Markets Always Rally Once the Event Is Behind Them
videos.description:
Stocks panicked overnight, then reversed and closed higher, and Cem Karsan of Kai Volatility has a blunt warning: don't attribute that to a macro narrative, because it has nothing to do with one. It's structural flows. Heading into any big event, skew runs toward record highs as everyone hedges. Once it resolves either way, the fear decays, those shorts get bought back, and the flows turn powerfully positive. Ilya Spivak backs it with the cleanest evidence available: Fed funds futures didn't move an inch.

videos.title: The Glass Half Full: When Will the Madness End? (Ep. 34)
videos.description:
In this episode of Glass Half Full, Ryan Detrick, Chief Market Strategist at Carson Group, and Sonu Varghese, Chief Macro Strategist at Carson Group, break down what the midterm elections could mean for the stock market, with just one week to go.

They start with what markets have been focused on: the AI wave, a possible rotation, and rising yields. Sonu explains why oil could be this year’s “October surprise,” with WTI crude at about $101 a barrel and Brent near $115 to $116. Ryan looks at history: over the last 23 midterms, the party that lost the White House gained House seats 20 times, by an average of about 29. Democrats are widely expected to take the House, while the Senate looks more competitive. The S&P 500 has also risen in each of the last 13 periods of split Congress.

Sonu then explains why Washington’s path of least resistance is more spending no matter who wins, which means more debt and potentially higher rates, but also more profits for the private sector in the short term. Ryan reminds listeners that stocks have done well under Obama, Trump 1.0, and Biden, even when many people disliked the president, and closes with a notable stat: the S&P 500 was higher 12 months after all 19 midterm elections since World War II. They still see a global bull market with life left in it, and encourage listeners to stick to their plan and go vote.

[Key Takeaways]
- Don’t let politics drive your investment plan. The stock market has done well under Obama, Trump 1.0, and Bide

stance.summary: Darius Dale is long-term bearish on US equities, warning that the current AI-driven capex bubble—the largest in economic history—will disrupt legacy industries and eventually trigger a historic secular bear market before or by the 2028 general election.

quotes.speaker: Darius Dale
quotes.text: Every capex bubble we've seen in the history of this economy and this is by far the biggest one, I think thanks to that work at Columbia Business School recently, this is by far the biggest capex bubble we've seen in economy. They all end in secular bear markets.

quotes.speaker: Darius Dale
quotes.text: And anytime you have a significant amount of change with legacy positioning, you have to go through the plumbing and the plumbing always leads downward. So you have to be very negative on this market cycle from a long-term perspective.

key_points.point: Companies are currently over-investing in AI compute and capex, creating uncertainty over whether profitability can be sustained by 2029 in a compute-abundant world.
The current capex bubble is the largest in economic history, and historically every major capex bubble ends in a secular bear market.
Significant innovation disrupts legacy industries and forces positioning adjustments through market plumbing that push prices downward.
While the market cycle has not peaked yet, the eventual peak will likely lead to a historic secular bear market.
The current market cycle will not survive past the 2028 US general election.
